summary: An FYI catalog that gives practical information for site administrators and network managers, describing tools for monitoring and debugging TCP/IP internets. It specifies no standard. It was replaced by RFC 1470.

eli5.summary: A shopping list of gadgets to check if your network is healthy and to find out what went wrong when it breaks.

questions: tools for debugging tcp ip networks
what is the network management tool catalog
what tools were available for tcp ip network management in 1990
how are network management tools categorized
subtitle: A practical catalog of tools for monitoring and debugging TCP/IP networks.

tldr.problem: Network administrators need a practical reference for tools to monitor TCP/IP networks, detect faults, and maintain system health, but available tools are scattered across vendors and implementations.
tldr.mechanism: This catalog compiles descriptions of network management tools available in 1990, categorizing them by function (monitoring, debugging, control), the resources they manage (IP, DECnet, bridges), and how they work (SNMP, CMIP, proprietary protocols).
tldr.outcome: The FYI provided a unified reference for site administrators choosing tools and highlighted gaps in available tooling. It was superseded by RFC 1470 with updated information.

today: RFC 1147 is Historic, superseded by RFC 1470 published in June 1993 with updated tool information. The specific tools and vendors described are from 1990 and are largely obsolete, but the catalog's framework for categorizing network management tools by function, mechanism, platform, and resource type established patterns that influenced network operations practices and tool development.

sections.title: What This Catalog Does
sections.content:
The Network Management Tool Catalog is a practical reference compiled by the IETF NOCTools Working Group in 1989. Its purpose is to fight the tendency to reinvent the wheel by pooling knowledge about available tools for managing TCP/IP networks and interconnected devices.

The catalog collects descriptions of tools used by site administrators and network managers to monitor system health, debug problems, and maintain networks. This is not a "how-to" manual on network management itself, but rather a reference for what tools exist and what they can do. Each tool entry is brief and focuses on practical use rather than serving as an operations manual.
sections.eli5: A list of tools network managers can use to check on their networks and fix problems when things go wrong. It was made by gathering information from tool developers and vendors so managers could see what was available.

sections.title: The Scope of Network Management
sections.content:
The catalog covers tools for managing TCP/IP networks and interconnected resources like local-area networks (LANs), routers, and wide-area network links. The tools described assume knowledge of the TCP/IP protocol suite and Internet architecture but do not require deep expertise to understand.

The catalog's tutorial section explains the core goals of network management: fault detection and diagnosis, configuration management with minimal disruption, measurement of resource utilization, and security. Network managers are evaluated on the availability and performance of their systems, so tools that detect and diagnose problems quickly are most valued.
sections.eli5: The tools are for managing networks that use TCP/IP and connected equipment like local networks and routers. They help network managers find and fix problems before users notice, and keep track of how much the network is being used.

sections.title: Tool Categories by Function
sections.content:
Tools are categorized by their primary function. Managers are distributed network management systems or system components that control multiple devices. Status tools remotely track the state of network components. Analyzers reconstruct and interpret protocol messages that span several packets, while Traffic tools monitor packet flow.

Specialized tools handle specific tasks: Debuggers generate arbitrary packets and monitor responses to drive components into various states, Benchmarks evaluate performance, Generators create test traffic, and Control tools change the state of remote resources. Routing tools discover packet routes, Maps discover and report system topology, References document configuration, Alarms trigger on events, and Security tools analyze or reduce security threats.
sections.eli5: Tools are divided by what they do: some watch the network for problems, some test how fast it runs, some send test messages, and some let managers fix things remotely. Special tools find which path packets take through the network or draw a map of how networks are connected.

sections.title: Network Resources and Protocol Suites
sections.content:
The catalog covers tools for different network protocols and resources. IP tools manage implementations of TCP/IP; OSI tools manage the ISO/OSI protocol suite; DECnet tools manage DEC's protocol suite. Specialized tools exist for specific services: DNS tools debug domain name systems, NFS tools debug network file systems, and SMTP tools debug mail transfer.

Hardware resources are also represented: tools manage Ethernet LANs, Token Ring LANs, FDDI networks, Bridges connecting LANs, and Star networks. Some tools work across multiple protocol suites and network types, while others are specialized for a single resource type.
sections.eli5: Tools are made for different types of networks: some work with IP networks, others with DECnet or OSI networks. There are also special tools just for checking domain names or file systems, and tools for different kinds of cables and connections like Ethernet or Token Ring.

sections.title: How Tools Gather Information
sections.content:
Tools use different mechanisms to monitor and manage networks. SNMP-based tools use the Simple Network Management Protocol to query agents on network devices; this is the dominant approach in the catalog. CMIP-based tools use the Common Management Information Protocol, based on ISO standards and providing a more comprehensive framework. Proprietary tools use vendor-specific communication techniques.

Other mechanisms include Ping-based tools that send ICMP echo probes to test reachability, Eavesdrop tools that passively monitor traffic (for example, by putting an Ethernet interface into promiscuous mode), and Spoof tools that test protocol implementations through peer-level message exchange. Tools may use the Curses terminal interface or X-Windows for display.
sections.eli5: Tools ask devices on the network for information using a standard protocol called SNMP, or they listen silently to traffic passing by. Some send test ping messages to see if hosts respond, and others send fake protocol messages to test how devices react.

sections.title: Platforms and Delivery Models
sections.content:
Tools run on different operating systems and hardware platforms. UNIX tools (4.xBSD and related systems) dominate the catalog. Many tools also run on VMS, DEC's operating system, or DOS on IBM personal computers. HP refers to Hewlett-Packard systems, and Macintosh tools run on Apple personal computers. Standalone tools are integrated hardware/software products requiring only a network interface.

Tools are distributed as Free software available at no charge, as commercial Products sold by vendors, or as source or library code. Some tools are packaged as Libraries with application programming interfaces or object-level subroutines that can be linked into other programs. Others are Source libraries (collections of source code subroutines) upon which developers can build other tools.
sections.eli5: Tools run on different computers: mainly UNIX workstations, but also on VAX machines, PC computers, and even Macintoshes. Some tools are free to download, some are sold by companies, and some are collections of code that programmers can use to build their own tools.

sections.title: Using the Catalog
sections.content:
The catalog organizes nearly 100 tools in alphabetical order by name. Each entry follows a standard format: Name and Keywords appear first, followed by an Abstract describing what the tool does and Mechanism explaining how it works. Caveats warn of special considerations, Bugs describe known issues, and Limitations state the boundaries of the tool's capabilities.

Practical information follows: Hardware Required and Software Required describe the environment needed, and Availability provides information on how to obtain the tool—online repositories, FTP addresses, or vendor contact details. Keywords also allow cross-comparison: tools are indexed by functional category, network type, mechanism, operating system, and acquisition type.
sections.eli5: Each tool has a description that says what it does, how it works, what computers it needs, and where to get it. There are also keyword tags so you can find all the tools that work with Ethernet, or all the free tools, or all the tools that use SNMP.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content:
RFC 1147 is an Informational FYI document published in April 1990 and is now Historic; it was superseded by RFC 1470, which provided an updated version with additional tools and refined descriptions as the field evolved. The specific tools and vendors listed in RFC 1147 are dated; many no longer exist or have been replaced.

However, the catalog's organizational structure and the types of tools it describes remain relevant to modern network operations. The categories of functionality (monitoring, debugging, control, analysis) and the mechanisms (SNMP and later protocols) established here became foundational patterns for network management tools. The document remains a historical snapshot of 1990s TCP/IP network management practices.
sections.eli5: This document was replaced by a newer version with updated information about tools. The specific tools in it are from 1990 and mostly don't exist anymore, but the ideas about what kinds of tools you need and how to organize them are still used today.
